texts.label: A
texts.title: Mill Street resurfacing: what to expect

paragraphs.text: Mill Street resurfacing: what to expect. Work begins on Monday 6 April and is expected to take four weeks, weather permitting. The street will stay open to pedestrians throughout, and to traffic in one direction only, from the square towards the river. Buses will be diverted along Chapel Road and will not call at the Mill Street stop; the nearest stop during the works is outside the health centre, about two hundred metres away.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Residents between numbers 2 and 60 will not be able to park on the street while their section is being surfaced. We will post a dated notice on your door three days before the machines reach you, and a temporary permit for the car park behind the library will be delivered with it. The permit is valid only for the dates printed on it. Vehicles left on a section that is being worked on will be moved to a nearby street, and the council will pay any charge that results.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Deliveries can still be made: drivers should use the square end of the street and the crew will let them through between jobs. Bin collections continue on the usual day, but bins must be left at the corner of Chapel Road rather than outside the house. Noisy work is limited to 8 am to 5 pm on weekdays and 9 am to 1 pm on Saturdays, with no work on Sundays. If you need to report a problem, the site office number is on the notice; calls out of hours go to the council switchboard.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Beech Court — laundry room. The laundry is in the basement and is open from 7 am to 10 pm every day. There are four washing machines and three dryers. Machines are booked on the sheet by the door in slots of ninety minutes, and no flat may book more than two slots in the same week. A slot not claimed within fifteen minutes may be taken by anyone waiting, so please cross your name out if your plans change.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Tokens cost £2.50 each and are bought from the machine in the entrance hall, which takes coins and cards but does not give change. One token runs a washing machine or a dryer for one cycle. The iron and board in the corner are free to use and must not be taken to flats. Please remove your washing promptly: items left more than an hour after a cycle ends are put in the basket by the sink, and the basket is emptied into the charity bin on the first of each month.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Dyeing, and washing anything covered in paint or oil, is not allowed in these machines, and the caretaker may charge for cleaning if it happens. Report a broken machine by writing on the sheet and telephoning the managing agent; do not open the door of a machine that has stopped mid-cycle. Children under twelve may not be in the laundry room without an adult. The room is cleaned on Wednesday mornings and the last booking before the cleaning is at 8 am.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Checkout training: your first week. You will spend the first two days beside an experienced colleague and will not serve customers alone until the trainer signs the checklist at the back of this booklet. The till is opened with your own code, which must not be shared, and closed whenever you leave the position, even for a moment. Every transaction is recorded against the code that was used, which protects you as much as the shop.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Most of the first week is about the things that go wrong rather than the things that go right. If a barcode will not scan, key in the number printed beneath it; if that fails, call a supervisor rather than guessing the price. Vouchers are scanned before payment, never after, and a voucher that has expired cannot be accepted even by a supervisor, because the till will not take it. Refunds are never processed at the checkout: send the customer to the service desk with the receipt.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Age-restricted goods are the part new staff find hardest. The rule is simple and absolute: if the customer looks under twenty-five, ask for identification, and accept only a passport, a driving licence or a card carrying the official hologram. If you are refused, or the identification looks wrong, decline the sale politely and call a supervisor; do not argue and do not explain your reasoning to the customer. A sale made without a check is a matter for the police as well as for the shop, and no manager will ask you to make one.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: At the end of a shift, count your float in the cash office with a second member of staff present, and sign the sheet together. Differences of a few pence are normal and are recorded, not investigated. A difference of more than ten pounds is looked into the same day, and you will be asked what happened rather than accused of anything; in practice most large differences turn out to be a miskeyed amount that can be found in the transaction log within minutes.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: D
texts.title: Travel and expenses: what the company pays

paragraphs.text: Travel and expenses: what the company pays. Book train tickets through the online portal at least seven days before travel where the journey is planned; tickets bought later are still paid for, but you may be asked why. Standard class is the default for journeys under three hours, and first class is allowed above that only when booked in advance and cheaper than a late standard fare. Taxis are for journeys where no public transport runs, for luggage that cannot be carried, or after 10 pm.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Accommodation is booked through the same portal, up to £120 a night outside the capital and £160 within it. Where you stay with family or friends instead, the company pays a flat £25 for each night as a contribution, with no receipt required. Breakfast is included in the room rate where the hotel offers it; where it does not, breakfast is claimed with the day’s meals. Personal items charged to the room, including films and the minibar, are never reimbursed.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Meals are claimed at actual cost with receipts, up to £8 for breakfast, £12 for lunch and £25 for dinner. Alcohol is not reimbursed, and a receipt that includes it should be annotated with the food total before it is submitted. Where a meal is provided at a conference, it may not also be claimed. Tips are reimbursed up to ten per cent of the food bill. Claims are made within thirty days of the journey; later claims need a line manager’s written approval and are paid with the following month’s salary.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Mileage in your own car is paid at the published rate per mile, which covers fuel, wear and insurance; you may not also claim for fuel. Parking and tolls are reimbursed with receipts, but parking fines never are, whatever the circumstances. If a journey is cancelled by the company, submit the unused ticket and the refund will be sought centrally; if you cancel for personal reasons, the ticket is your own cost. Anything not covered by these rules should be agreed with your manager before it is spent, not after.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: E
texts.title: When the streets first lit up

paragraphs.text: It is difficult now to imagine a city in which going out after dark was a decision rather than a habit. Before the eighteenth century, most European towns were dark once the sun went down, and the people who moved through them carried their own light or hired someone to carry it for them. Curfews were common and were as much about visibility as about order: a town that could not see its streets preferred everyone to be indoors.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first public lighting was a tax on householders rather than a service from the council. Cities ordered every household on a main street to hang a lantern outside between certain hours on moonless nights, and fined those who did not. The results were uneven, since a lantern is only as reliable as the person filling it, but the principle mattered: for the first time the street itself, rather than the traveller, was expected to be lit. Oil lamps on posts followed, tended by lamplighters who walked a fixed round twice a day.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Gas changed the scale of the thing. The first gas-lit street appeared in London in 1807, and within thirty years most large European cities had networks of pipes and cast-iron posts. Gas was brighter than oil, could be turned on centrally, and made possible a genuinely new thing: a lit street that did not depend on anyone walking along it. It also required an industry — works, pipes, meters, men — and the cost was carried by the city, which is one reason lighting spread outwards from the districts where the wealthy lived.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: What the light did to behaviour is harder to measure than the engineers assumed. Shopkeepers stayed open later, theatres moved their performances, and evening classes became possible for people who worked during the day; all of that is documented. The effect on crime is less clear. Contemporary accounts credited lighting with emptying the streets of thieves, and modern reviews of lighting schemes find real but modest reductions in some kinds of offence and none in others. What lighting reliably changes is how safe people feel, which is not the same thing and is not nothing.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Electricity arrived at the end of the nineteenth century and won more slowly than the histories suggest. Early arc lamps were too bright for a street and were installed on towers that lit whole districts at once, producing a hard glare and deep shadows that nobody liked. Gas lighting improved in response, with a mantle that trebled its brightness, and the two systems competed for four decades. Some cities were still lighting streets with gas in the 1950s, and a few kept gas lamps in historic districts on purpose, where they remain.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The current change is quieter and larger than either. Sodium lamps, which made cities orange for half a century, are being replaced by light-emitting diodes, which use a fraction of the power and can be dimmed or switched by the hour. The saving is real: a medium-sized town can cut its lighting bill by two thirds. The difficulty is that the new lamps are usually whiter and more directional, and a white light of the same measured brightness looks glaring and casts sharper shadows, so the first replacements produced more complaints than the old lamps ever had.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Astronomers and biologists have added an argument that did not exist before. Light spilling upwards has made the night sky invisible from most cities, and light at night disturbs insects, birds and plants in ways that are now well documented; the moths circling a lamp are the visible part of a much larger effect. Because modern lamps can be aimed and dimmed, the remedy is cheaper than it was: shielding the fitting, lowering the output after midnight, and using warmer colours all reduce the harm without leaving anyone in the dark.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The argument about street lighting has therefore turned around. For two centuries the question was how to get more light into the street; it is now how much light is enough, and where it should not go. That is a harder question, because it has no single answer: a shopping street, a residential road and a park each want something different, and the same lamp cannot be right for all of them. The one thing the long history suggests is that the standard eventually settles at whatever people are used to, which is an argument for choosing carefully now.
paragraphs.label: H
